evals.name: fuel-trim-differential-diagnosis
evals.prompt: Pulled logs off my 4.0 V6 this weekend (stock, 190k miles, no mods). Warm idle in park: bank 1 STFT bouncing around +3%, LTFT sitting at +19%. Bank 2 is basically identical. At 45 mph steady cruise LTFT is down to +6% and STFT +2%. On a hard pull both trims go to 0 and stay there. No codes, MIL is off, and fuel pressure at idle reads spec on a gauge. What's actually going on here and what should I check first?
evals.expected_output: Reads the SHAPE, not the number: large at idle and shrinking as load/airflow rises = an additive / fixed-quantity error (unmetered air), not a multiplicative/scaling error (MAF calibration, fuel pressure, injector flow), which would hold roughly constant in percent across load. Both banks equal points at a shared source rather than a bank-specific part. Notes trims going to 0 under a hard pull is OPEN LOOP, not the fault resolving, and carries no diagnostic information. Flags purge duty and an upstream exhaust leak as classic confounders. Notes LTFT +19% is approaching typical adaptation authority. Prescribes a differential check and says what re-logging should show if the hypothesis is right.
assertions: Identifies the trim-vs-load shape (large at idle, shrinking with load) as a fixed-quantity/additive error — unmetered air — rather than a scaling error
Explicitly rules out or deprioritizes scaling causes (MAF calibration, fuel pressure, injector flow) using the fact that they would hold roughly constant in percent across load
States that trims reading 0 under the hard pull is open loop, not the fault resolving, and carries no diagnostic information
Uses both-banks-equal to point at a shared source (plenum, PCV, brake booster, purge, MAF) rather than bank-specific hardware
Names at least two confounders that mimic this pattern (EVAP purge, upstream exhaust leak, adaptation reset, MAF pulsation) before diagnosing hardware
Notes that 'no codes' does not exclude the fault — these failures are electrically perfect
Gives a concrete first check (smoke/vacuum test, purge commanded closed, PCV) and states what re-logging should show if the hypothesis holds
Does not state a universal numeric DTC threshold for P0171/P0174 as if it were standardized

evals.name: wot-fuel-correction-magnitude
evals.prompt: I've got a wideband and I'm datalogging WOT pulls in 3rd on my NA build. The tune targets 12.8 AFR at WOT. From 3000-4000 rpm I'm measuring right on 12.8, but above 4500 I'm reading 13.6-13.9. I'm at about 6800 ft elevation. Injectors are 550cc at 43.5 psi base and the log shows 78% duty at redline. Should I just add 7% fuel to the top of the VE table?
evals.expected_output: Does not accept the framing. Separates the two candidate causes that produce an identical lean-at-high-rpm trace: a VE/airflow model error versus running out of fuel DELIVERY (rail pressure falling at high flow, injectors near their usable limit) — distinguished by whether rail pressure holds at WOT. Sizes the correction from the measured/target ratio per rpm bin rather than a whole-pull average. Notes ~6800 ft is about 79-80 kPa, which changes airflow and duty math but not the AFR target. Raises measurement validity and prescribes a re-log.
assertions: Does not simply endorse adding 7%; presents VE/airflow error and fuel-delivery shortfall as competing causes of the same lean-at-high-rpm trace
Names the discriminating measurement — whether rail/fuel pressure holds at high rpm WOT (or an equivalent delivery check)
Sizes the correction from the measured-to-target ratio in engineering units (roughly 6-8%) and applies it only to the affected rpm/load cells rather than to a whole-pull average
Treats altitude correctly: ~6800 ft is roughly 79-80 kPa ambient, which affects airflow, power, and duty-cycle math but does NOT change the AFR/lambda target
Raises measurement validity — wideband response lag or placement, channel alignment at high rpm, and that a single pull is not a dataset
Prescribes a re-log to validate the change and states what a successful correction should look like
Does not assert that 78% injector duty by itself proves the injectors are out of capacity

evals.name: boost-taper-no-codes
evals.prompt: 2.0T, tune targets 18 psi. Datalog shows boost peaking at 18.2 psi around 3500 rpm then falling off to 14.5 psi by 6500. Wastegate duty is at 92% at 6500. IATs climb from 38C at the start of the pull to 68C at the end. Timing is about 4 degrees lower at 6000 rpm than in a log I took back in spring. No codes. Ambient was 95F. Is my turbo dying?
evals.expected_output: Uses duty cycle as the control-effort channel: 92% with boost still falling means the boost controller is out of authority (leak, gate, or compressor past its efficient flow), NOT the ECU deliberately limiting, which would show LOW duty with the same boost trace. Identifies 68C IAT as heat soak and the likely cause of the timing being down, so the 4-degree delta versus a spring log is confounded by charge temperature and 95F ambient and is not evidence of turbo failure. Reasons in absolute pressure / pressure ratio. Prescribes discriminating next steps.
assertions: Reads 92% wastegate duty as the control effort saturating — the boost controller is out of authority
Explicitly contrasts saturated duty versus low duty as opposite diagnoses producible from the same boost trace
Attributes the 4-degree timing reduction primarily to charge temperature (68C IAT) and 95F ambient rather than to turbo failure
States that comparing this log against the spring log is confounded by ambient and charge temperature, so the timing delta is not evidence
Reasons about boost in absolute pressure or pressure ratio rather than gauge psi when comparing across conditions
Answers the user's actual question — turbo failure is not established — instead of only listing observations
Prescribes discriminating next steps including a boost leak check (justified by the saturated duty) and a back-to-back log at comparable IAT/ambient
Notes that high-rpm boost taper is partly expected rather than treating any taper as a fault

evals.name: spark-advance-high-rpm-sanity
evals.prompt: NA 3.5 V6 on pump 91, no knock events logged anywhere. WOT timing from my log: 22° at 2000, 29° at 3000, 33° at 4000, 35° at 5000, 36° at 6000. A buddy says combustion takes a fixed ~2 ms so advance should scale linearly with rpm — about 0.012 × rpm, so ~70° at 6000 — and that my tune is leaving a ton of power on the table up top. Should I add 10-15° above 5000?
evals.expected_output: No. The fixed-time burn model is wrong above low speed: turbulence and flame speed scale with piston speed, so burn duration is nearly constant in crank degrees (growing only ~rpm^0.2-0.35) and MBT advance flattens at high rpm — the logged curve's shape is normal, and ~70° at 6000 would be absurd. MBT is a flat optimum (several degrees of retard ≈ 1 % torque), so even if timing were a few degrees short the gain would be small. Zero knock events are only reassuring if the knock channel is live and enabled. The way to find out is a controlled spark sweep in a few cells (small steps, watching knock and measuring torque/acceleration with repeat runs), not a blanket +10-15°.
assertions: Rejects the fixed-2-ms / 0.012 × rpm model, explaining that burn duration is roughly constant in crank angle because flame speed rises with turbulence/piston speed
States that the logged curve flattening at high rpm is normal and that ~70° at 6000 rpm is not a realistic target
Notes that MBT is a flat optimum, so a few degrees short of MBT costs only around 1 % torque
Does not recommend adding 10-15° across the top end
Recommends a controlled, incremental spark test (small steps, knock monitored, repeated runs or a torque/acceleration measure) instead
Treats 'no knock events logged' as meaningful only if the knock channel is live/enabled, or otherwise notes the knock-limited ceiling

evals.name: pd-supercharger-boost-at-altitude
evals.prompt: Just finished a roots-type supercharger install (Eaton TVS) on my V6 — the kit is advertised at 7 psi. I live at about 6,500 ft and my boost gauge only shows 5.4-5.6 psi at WOT, flat from ~2500 rpm up. IATs look fine. Is the belt slipping or is the bypass valve stuck? Should I go down a pulley size to get my 7 psi?
evals.expected_output: Probably neither. A positive-displacement blower multiplies ambient pressure — it holds a roughly constant pressure ratio, not a gauge pressure. 7 psi at sea level is PR ≈ 1.48; at ~80 kPa ambient (6,500 ft) that is ~118 kPa absolute ≈ 5.5 psi gauge, exactly what the gauge shows. Flat boost from low rpm is the normal PD shape. Belt slip would show boost sagging at high rpm and varying pull to pull; a stuck-open bypass would leave airflow per rev near NA. Discriminate with airflow per rev (MAF g/rev) vs expectation and repeat pulls. Going down a pulley raises PR, blower speed, discharge temperature and knock risk and requires a retune (fuel and timing), and on a returnless fuel system increases the ΔP deficit — it is a calibration decision, not a fix for a fault.
assertions: Explains that a positive-displacement supercharger delivers a roughly constant pressure ratio, so gauge boost falls with ambient pressure at altitude
Shows or states that 7 psi at sea level corresponds to roughly 5.5 psi gauge (~118 kPa absolute) at ~80 kPa / 6,500 ft
Concludes the reading is consistent with a healthy system and does not diagnose belt slip or a stuck bypass from it
Names what belt slip or a stuck-open bypass would actually look like (e.g. boost sagging at high rpm / varying pull to pull; WOT airflow per rev near NA)
Says a smaller pulley is a calibration change requiring a retune (fuel and timing), with more heat and knock risk and blower-speed limits to check, not a repair

evals.name: purge-split-pulse-and-trim
evals.prompt: Port-injected V6, factory ECU, closed loop. I'm checking my injector model by comparing the logged pulse width to what I compute from MAF airflow and the injector constant. On steady cruise the logged pulse comes out 5-10% shorter than my model on some drives and dead on in others, and the long-term trims are exactly 0.0% on both banks after three weeks of mostly 10-minute town trips. No codes, and I haven't touched the fuel system. Is the injector constant wrong, and is the ECU just refusing to learn?
evals.expected_output: Splits by purge state before blaming the injector model. Many ECUs cut the injector pulse by a purge factor of their own while purging (they estimate the vapor they are ingesting), so a pulse-versus-airflow check made on purging cruise reads 5-10% short and on purge-off cruise reads right; that pattern is the purge factor, not a wrong injector constant, and the check should be run on purge-off samples (or carry purge state as a covariate). Trims at exactly 0.0% on both banks are a stronger fault signal than +/-8%, but there is a fifth cause beside the usual four (codes cleared, adaptation reset, loop not closed, channel not live): adaptation can be gated on purge, with learning allowed only after the canister has been cleaned out within the current engine start, or only in purge-off phases, and a run of short trips never opens that gate. So zeros here may be a driving pattern, not a fault. Says what to log or do next: purge duty/state alongside trims and pulse, one longer drive with sustained purge (or whatever the gate needs), and trims reported split by purge state; notes a learned cell may have been learned with vapor in it. Does not recommend changing the injector constant.
assertions: Splits the pulse-versus-airflow comparison by purge state, or carries purge as a covariate, before drawing any conclusion about the injector model
Says a purge factor applied by the ECU to the injector pulse reads as a 5-10% pulse or injector-model error on purging samples and disappears with purge off
Does not recommend changing the injector constant or MAF scaling from the purging samples

Identifies that exactly 0.0% trims after weeks of short trips can be a learning gate (adaptation allowed only after enough purge or only in purge-off phases) that short trips never open, in addition to the other causes of zero trim (codes or adaptation just cleared, loop not closed, channel not live)

Does not call the zero trims a healthy result or a fault by itself, and says what to log next (purge state alongside trims and pulse) and what a longer drive or purge-off re-log should show if the gate hypothesis is right
Notes that any learned trim cell may have been learned with vapor in it, and that trims should be reported split by purge state before their shape is read

evals.name: three-instruments-same-sensor
evals.prompt: I'm validating a new wideband reading from my ECU's data stream. I have three things that all agree to within 1% across a drive: the AFR my scan tool shows, the lambda PID the ECU reports, and the raw O2 sensor voltage DID converted with the textbook formula. Closed-loop cruise sits right on target. That's three independent instruments agreeing, so I'm going to call the sensor calibration verified and use it to size a fuel table change for wide-open throttle. Any reason not to?
evals.expected_output: Does not accept 'three independent instruments'. Independence means different sensors: count sensors, not channels. The scan-tool AFR, the ECU's lambda PID and the sensor-voltage DID all come from the one upstream probe read three ways, so their agreement validates the decoding and unit conversion, not the sensor. Agreement at closed-loop cruise with the target is also circular: the fuel controller drives that sensor's reading to the target whatever the sensor's error, so on target proves the loop works, not that the sensor is right. A wideband's gain error shows away from lambda = 1 (WOT, fuel cut), exactly where the table change is going. And a third-party conversion of the raw voltage skips whatever compensation the ECU applies (barometric or exhaust-pressure gain), so the channels can differ by a scale factor with nothing wrong. A genuinely independent check needs a second sensor (an external wideband bolted in the exhaust) or a quantity that doesn't pass through that sensor (fuel flow against measured airflow), or a fuel-cut free-air check of the gain. Recommends not sizing a WOT edit from this sensor alone yet and says what measurement would separate sensor error from delivery error.
assertions: States that the three channels are one sensor read three ways and are not independent instruments (count sensors, not channels)
Explains that agreement with target at closed-loop cruise is circular because the controller steers this sensor's reading to the target
Notes that wideband gain error shows away from lambda = 1 (WOT, fuel cut), where cruise agreement says nothing, and that WOT is where the edit is being sized

Notes that a tool which converts the raw voltage itself can skip a compensation the ECU applies (barometric or exhaust-pressure gain), so channels can disagree by a scale factor with nothing wrong, or agree while both are wrong
Names a genuinely independent check: a second probe or external wideband, a fuel-flow against airflow check that bypasses the sensor, or a free-air reading in fuel cut
Does not endorse sizing a WOT fuel table change from this evidence alone

evals.name: idle-only-lean-trim-follows-heat
evals.prompt: My engine shows a lean idle trim that looks like a vacuum leak by the book: total trim about +8% at warm idle, shrinking to roughly zero by light cruise, both banks the same, purge off, no codes. But the same idle logged on a cool morning at around 20 C intake was about 0%. I'm planning to add a fixed amount of fuel in the idle cells sized from yesterday's hot-afternoon log to cancel the +8%. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: Not yet. The additive shape (big at idle, shrinking with load, both banks equal) fits a leak, but a fixed leak would not change between a cool morning and a hot afternoon, so the idle trim moving with temperature is the discriminating fact: it has the leak's shape without being a fixed quantity. Candidates are heat-related: hot fuel and rail-pressure sag or vapor, hot air at the meter or intake-temperature compensation, heat soak at idle where airflow is low. Compares idle trim at matched intake temperature and matched rail pressure across sessions (purge off in all of them) before calling a leak or sizing anything. A fixed idle edit sized from one hot drive would be wrong on every cool day. A smoke test is still cheap and would rule a leak in or out directly. States what each hypothesis predicts: a true leak gives similar idle trim cool and hot, a heat effect tracks intake temperature or rail pressure. Does not make the edit from one session.
assertions: Recognizes that the idle trim differing between a cool and a hot session is inconsistent with a fixed-quantity leak and treats temperature (or rail pressure) as a candidate cause
Recommends comparing idle trims at matched intake temperature and matched rail pressure across sessions, with purge state held the same, before sizing anything
Does not recommend a fixed idle fuel correction sized from a single hot-afternoon log
States what a real leak versus a heat effect would each predict in the next log (leak: similar trim cool and hot; heat: trim tracks intake temperature or rail pressure)
May still offer a smoke or vacuum test as a cheap direct check, without treating the trim shape alone as proof of a leak
